meanings: to be, to exist, to live

examples.japanese: 家の近くに新しいカフェがあります。
examples.furigana: 家[いえ]の 近[ちか]くに 新[あたら]しいカフェがあります。
examples.romaji: ie no chikaku ni atarashii kafe ga arimasu.
examples.english: There's a new café near my house.

examples.japanese: 来週、日本語のテストがあるんだ。
examples.furigana: 来週[らいしゅう]、 日本語[にほんご]のテストがあるんだ。
examples.romaji: raishuu, nihongo no tesuto ga aru nda.
examples.english: You see, I have a Japanese test next week.

usage_notes: Used for the existence of inanimate things, plants, and events (パーティーがある). For people and animals, use いる instead. The plain negative is irregular: ない / ありません, never あらない. The thing that exists is marked with が, and the place with に.

examples.japanese: コーヒーはあんまり飲みません。
examples.furigana: コーヒーはあんまり 飲[の]みません。
examples.romaji: koohii wa anmari nomimasen.
examples.english: I don't drink much coffee.

examples.japanese: あんまり食べると、眠くなるよ。
examples.furigana: あんまり 食[た]べると、 眠[ねむ]くなるよ。
examples.romaji: anmari taberu to, nemuku naru yo.
examples.english: If you eat too much, you'll get sleepy.

usage_notes: あんまり is the conversational form of あまり. It is usually used adverbially, not as a な-adjective. With a negative predicate, it means “not very” or “not much” (あんまり食べない). In casual affirmative sentences, it can mean “too much,” often as あんまり〜と or あんまり〜から.

usage_notes: Everyday word for a chair or stool; often written 椅子 in kanji. You sit down on one with に: いすに座る. Chairs are counted with 〜脚(きゃく) or informally 〜つ. The "post/position" sense is figurative (大臣のいす = a minister's seat) and is normally written in kanji, so beginners can treat いす as simply "chair."

usage_notes: An ichidan verb, so かけます・かけない・かけた・かけて. The dictionary entry looks huge, but beginners really only need a handful of set collocations: 電話をかける (make a call), 音楽/CDをかける (play music), めがねをかける (wear glasses), かぎをかける (lock up), 時間/お金をかける (spend time/money), しょうゆをかける (pour soy sauce on). Note the intransitive partner かかる: you かける a call, but 電話がかかってくる (a call comes in), and 時間がかかる means "it takes time" while 時間をかける means "to devote time to it." In casual speech the を is often dropped: 電話かけたよ.

usage_notes: 帰る is used for returning to a place you belong — home, your hometown, your own country — so 家に帰る, 国に帰る, 実家に帰る. Use 戻る for coming back to a place you are only temporarily at (e.g. returning to the office). Although it ends in -eru, it is a godan verb: negative 帰らない, past 帰った, て-form 帰って; 帰れる is the potential ('can go home'). The destination takes に or へ.

usage_notes: Almost always used as ...と思う: the thought or opinion comes first in plain (short) form, followed by と思います, even when the rest of the sentence is polite. 思う is transitive and takes を with noun objects (何を思っていますか), but for stating opinions the と pattern is the normal one. For present-moment thoughts about oneself, 思っている is also common (ずっとそう思っています, "I've thought so all along").

usage_notes: Godan verb: 歌わない・歌います・歌った・歌って, potential 歌える. What you sing takes を, and 歌を歌う ("sing a song") is the normal collocation, not redundant; the place or accompaniment takes で (カラオケで, ギターで). 歌 is the noun "song"; the same kanji read うた.

usage_notes: 歌手 is the everyday word for a professional singer; a hobbyist who just likes singing is 歌が好きな人, not 歌手. The 手 here is the しゅ of occupations (運転手 driver, 選手 athlete), so it means "the person who does it" rather than "hand." Common collocations: 歌手になる (become a singer), 好きな歌手 (a singer one likes).

usage_notes: Intransitive: the thing itself stops (電車が止まる). To stop something yourself, use the transitive pair 止める(とめる): 車を止める. 止まっている / 止まってる describes the resulting state — "is stopped, is at a standstill" (時計が止まってる = the clock has stopped). Note the homophone 泊まる (to stay overnight), and that rain or noise ceasing normally takes 止む(やむ), not 止まる.

examples.japanese: 明日までにこのプログラムを直すのは無理です。
examples.furigana: 明日[あした]までにこのプログラムを 直[なお]すのは 無理[むり]です。

examples.romaji: Gomen, shuumatsu wa muri nan da.

usage_notes: 無理です is the standard soft way to turn something down — it says "that can't be done" without a blunt いいえ. As a suru verb, 無理する means to push yourself too hard, and 無理しないで(ください) is a very common way to say "don't overdo it / take care of yourself." The adverbial 無理に means "forcibly, against one's will," as in 無理に食べなくてもいいよ.

examples.japanese: この店では、古い物が安く買えます。
examples.furigana: この 店[みせ]では、 古[ふる]い 物[もの]が 安[やす]く 買[か]えます。

examples.romaji: Yama ni motte iku mono, mou kimeta?
examples.english: Have you already decided what to take up the mountain?

usage_notes: 物 is a physical thing you can touch; for intangible matters, facts, or experiences use こと (例: 大事な物 = a valuable object, 大事なこと = an important matter). It is very often written in kana as もの, and it appears in many compounds like 食べ物, 飲み物, 買い物. Note that the homophone 者 (もの) means "person" and is a separate word.

examples.japanese: 新しいアルバムの中で、この曲が特に好きです。
examples.furigana: 新[あたら]しいアルバムの 中[なか]で、 この 曲[きょく]が 特[とく]に 好[す]きです。
examples.romaji: Atarashii arubamu no naka de, kono kyoku ga toku ni suki desu.
examples.english: Out of the new album, I especially like this song.

examples.japanese: 今週末は特に予定ないんだ。
examples.furigana: 今週末[こんしゅうまつ]は 特[とく]に 予定[よてい]ないんだ。
examples.romaji: Konshuumatsu wa toku ni yotei nai n da.
examples.english: I don't have any particular plans this weekend.

usage_notes: 特に is an adverb that singles out one thing from a larger group, so it often follows a general statement (「日本料理が好きですが、特に寿司が…」). With a negative it means "not particularly / nothing in particular": 特に予定はない, 特に問題ありません. Don't confuse it with the な-adjective 特別な ("special"), which describes a noun rather than modifying a verb or adjective.

examples.japanese: 今日は特別なメニューがあります。
examples.furigana: 今日[きょう]は 特別[とくべつ]なメニューがあります。
examples.romaji: kyou wa tokubetsu na menyuu ga arimasu.
examples.english: Today there is a special menu.

examples.japanese: 誕生日だから、特別なケーキを作ったんだ。
examples.furigana: 誕生日[たんじょうび]だから、 特別[とくべつ]なケーキを 作[つく]ったんだ。
examples.romaji: tanjoubi da kara, tokubetsu na keeki o tsukutta n da.
examples.english: It's her birthday, so I made a special cake.

usage_notes: な-adjective: 特別な + noun (特別な日 "a special day"), and 特別に + verb when it modifies an action (特別に作る "make it specially"). It can also stand alone as a noun, as in 特別なことじゃない "it's nothing special." Don't confuse it with the adverb 特に, which means "especially, particularly" and never takes な.

examples.romaji: Kare ga konakatta riyuu, shitteru?

usage_notes: 理由 is the reason or motive behind someone's action or decision, and it often appears as 「理由は〜からです」 ("The reason is that…") or after a plain-form clause, as in 休んだ理由 ("the reason I took the day off"). For the physical or technical cause of a problem or accident, Japanese prefers 原因(げんいん) instead.

usage_notes: Everyday word for buying: 〜を買う, with the place marked by で (スーパーで買う). As a godan verb: 買います / 買わない / 買った / 買って. Note the わ in the negative 買わない, not 買あない. The extra meanings ('to value highly', as in 高く買う, or 'to provoke', as in 恨みを買う) are set phrases you can leave for later.

usage_notes: 走る looks like a ru-verb but is a u-verb: 走らない・走ります・走った・走って, potential 走れる. It is intransitive, so the person or thing running is marked by が/は; the route or place you run through takes を (公園を走る "run through the park"), while 走りに行く means "go for a run." It also describes vehicles moving along: 電車が走っている.

usage_notes: 起きる is an ichidan intransitive verb: 起きます、起きない、起きた、起きて. It covers both getting out of bed and being/staying awake (まだ起きています = "I'm still up"). The transitive partner is 起こす, "to wake someone up" (母が私を起こしました). Note also the third meaning, "to happen," used mostly of bad events: 事故が起きました。

The everyday way to say you own a pet is the ている form: 犬を飼っています / 飼ってる (an ongoing state), not the plain 飼います. Note the homophone 買う (to buy) — same かう, different kanji.

usage_notes: Note the reading: 魚 is うお (not さかな) inside this compound, and 市場 is いちば — a physical marketplace you can walk through. 市場 read しじょう means "market" in the economic sense (株式市場, the stock market), so don't mix the two. Big wholesale fish markets like Toyosu are typical referents; for a fish counter in a supermarket you'd just say 魚屋 or 魚のコーナー.
